title: Tablet XII: an appended translation
short: Tablet XII is a translation of the second half of a Sumerian poem; it does not continue Tablet XI, and Enkidu is alive in it.
body: The Sumerian poem 'Bilgames, Enkidu and the Netherworld' tells how two wooden objects made from Inanna's tree, the pukku and mekku (probably a ball and mallet, or a drum and drumstick), fell into the underworld. Tablet XII translates the second half of that poem into Akkadian, beginning at the moment the objects fall. Thompson rendered the words as 'seine' and 'net', fishing gear, an older guess, and his 'Architect' is the nagaru, a carpenter, in whose house the objects lay. Because Enkidu is alive here, though he died in Tablet VII, most scholars, including George, treat the tablet as an appendix added to the eleven-tablet poem; others argue that its account of the dead was deliberately attached as an epilogue to the theme of mortality. Thompson's note remarks that the previous tablet ended with the description of Uruk.

title: The rules for visiting the underworld
short: Gilgamish tells Enkidu not to wear clean clothes or oil, nor to carry a bow or stick, nor to kiss his wife: the dead will recognise him.
body: Enkidu offers to go down to fetch the lost objects, and Gilgamish instructs him how to behave in the underworld: no clean clothes, no sweet oil, no bow, no stick, no sandals, no kissing or striking of wife and child. These are the signs of a living person, which would make the dead recognise and seize him. The rules reverse normal life and resemble mourning customs, in which the living avoid washing and fine clothes. Thompson's note admits that the opening lines allow two restorations. Enkidu breaks every rule, as the following lines show item by item, and is held fast by the underworld.

title: The mother of Ninazu
short: The dead mother of Ninazu, whose shoulders are bare, is Ereshkigal mourning.
body: Ninazu was a god of the underworld and of healing, and his mother is usually identified as Ereshkigal, the queen of the dead. The short dirge-like lines describe her lying unclothed, her shoulders bare and her breast uncovered, an image of the underworld queen in mourning, perhaps for her dead husband. Thompson set these lines as a separate short-lined lyric, distinct from his hexameters. The refrain is repeated after Enkidu breaks the rules: 'the mourning of earth' holds him fast.

title: Namtar
short: Namtar ('Fate') is the plague-demon and minister of Ereshkigal.
body: Namtar, whose Sumerian name means 'fate' or 'destiny', was a demon of plague and death and the vizier of Ereshkigal, queen of the underworld; in the myth of Nergal and Ereshkigal he acts as her messenger. Thompson glosses him in the line as 'the Plague-god'. Gilgamish's point is that Enkidu was not taken by any of the normal agents of death, so he can still be retrieved. The list of possible causes (plague, fever, demon, battle) summarises the ways a Mesopotamian could die.

title: Nergal 'the Croucher'
short: The 'Croucher' (rabisu) is a lurking demon; Thompson takes it with Nergal.
body: Thompson's 'the Croucher' renders rabisu, 'the Lurker', a demon that lies in wait. Thompson attaches the term to Nergal, 'the ruthless', god of plague and king of the underworld (husband of Ereshkigal). Elsewhere rabisu is a separate class of demon; the line is open to both readings. The same Nergal appears at the end of the tablet as 'the warrior-hero' who opens a hole in the earth: the god of death becomes the agent of a brief reunion.

title: 'Only the earth seized him'
short: Enkidu was taken not by Namtar or Nergal, nor in battle: 'the earth seized him'.
body: Thompson's note gives the literal 'twas the earth [seized h]im'. The refrain insists that Enkidu did not die of disease (Namtar, fever), nor at the hands of the death-demon, nor in battle: the underworld simply kept him because he broke its taboos. Gilgamish repeats the plea three times, to Enlil, to the Moon-god and to Ea, in identical words, a typical triple repetition. In this tablet Enkidu's fate is a punishment for imprudence, not the result of the gods' sentence as in Tablet VII, another sign that the tablet has a separate origin.

title: Ekur
short: Ekur was Enlil's temple at Nippur.
body: Ekur ('Mountain House') was Enlil's temple at Nippur, the religious centre of Sumer. Gilgamish appeals in turn to Enlil, to Sin the Moon-god, and to Ea, calling each 'Father'. Enlil and Sin give no answer; Ea, the friend of mankind, responds, as he did in the Flood story. The sequence of three appeals with identical wording is typical of Sumerian narrative style, and reflects the Sumerian original of this tablet.

title: Nergal opens a hole
short: Ea commands Nergal to open a hole so that Enkidu's ghost can rise.
body: Ea orders Nergal, 'the warrior-hero', to open a hole in the earth so that Enkidu's spirit can come up and speak with his 'brother'. In the Sumerian original it is Utu, the sun-god, who opens the hole, appropriately, since the sun was thought to pass through the underworld at night; the Akkadian version gives the role to Nergal, king of the underworld. Thompson restores part of the passage, as his brackets show. The two friends embrace and 'commune together, mourning'.

title: The ghost like a wind
short: Enkidu's ghost rises like a breath of wind.
body: Enkidu's ghost (utukku) rises 'like a breath of wind' (zaqiqu), a common image of the insubstantial spirit of the dead. The image is close to the Homeric picture of Patroclus' ghost, which Akhilleus cannot embrace and which vanishes 'like smoke' (Iliad 23.99-101); in the Akkadian text the friends do embrace, but the conversation that follows is full of sorrow. Thompson's 'spirit' renders the Akkadian term for a ghost.

title: The laws of the underworld
short: Enkidu reports on the conditions of the dead.
body: Gilgamish asks his friend to tell him the 'order' of the underworld. Enkidu refuses, then tells him to sit and weep: the friend's body Gilgamish once caressed is eaten by vermin and full of dust. A catalogue follows of different classes of the dead and their fates, answered in a fixed formula ('Didst thou see him?' 'I saw'). Thompson's text preserves only part of the catalogue; the Sumerian original is longer, contrasting the man with seven sons, who sits among the gods, with the childless and the unburied.

anchor: hath the worm made its entry
title: The worm
short: The worm consumes the body Gilgamish touched.
body: Enkidu's description of his own body, like an old garment eaten by the worm and filled with dust, is one of the bleakest images in the epic. Thompson restores the words 'friend' and 'bride' in square brackets. In George's edition the passage refers to Enkidu's own body ('my body, which you touched'). The image recalls the maggot that fell from Enkidu's corpse in Tablet X, and it makes physical decay the final revelation of the underworld. Gilgamish's quest for life ends with this knowledge.

title: The hero slain in battle
body: The man killed in battle is shown honoured in the underworld: his parents tend his head and his wife weeps over him. Thompson's notes give the literal 'his father and his mother' and 'o'er him his wife'. Status among the dead depends on manner of death, number of sons, and above all burial and the continuing offerings of descendants. The heroic ideal of Tablet III, a name won in battle, thus survives in a muted form even in the underworld.

anchor: He whose corpse in desert lieth
title: The unburied dead
short: The ghost of the unburied finds no rest.
body: The ghost of a man whose corpse lies unburied in the open country finds no rest in the earth. Proper burial was essential in Mesopotamian belief, as in Greek: compare Patroclus' ghost in Iliad 23, who begs Akhilleus for burial so that he may pass the gates of Hades. The line is a sombre reminder of the many travellers and soldiers who died far from home, and of Gilgamish's own long refusal to bury Enkidu (X).

title: The untended ghost
short: The ghost with no one to make offerings eats scraps thrown in the street.
body: The last line of the epic's twelfth tablet describes the ghost with no one to make funerary offerings (kispu): it eats scraps from the pot and crusts of bread thrown into the street. Regular offerings of food and water by descendants sustained the dead; without them a ghost might haunt the living. The epic thus ends not with Gilgamish's glory but with the most wretched of the dead, an ending that emphasises the importance of family and memory, and perhaps of the name preserved in writing.
